student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. The audience spans the three levels of the organization's AI taxonomy, and a single course serves all three: Operators (limited end-user interaction with the AI; need to accurately interpret outputs and ensure the technology enhances rather than replaces judgement); Contributors (interact with the AI but do not make decisions about the technology); and Shapers (interact with the AI and hold decision-making capacity).
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness; mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in informatics fluency; assume no prior training in health data standards. Learners engage best with REAL record examples — actual note text, lab values with their metadata, imaging headers — not abstract definitions. Plain language, terms defined on first use, short daily sessions.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This module teaches CLINICAL RECORDS: what the medical record is, the types of records (EHR notes, laboratory results, medical imaging, medication data), the metadata and provenance that make a recorded value interpretable, and the standards that structure records — FHIR for exchange, OMOP for research, LOINC for laboratory observations, SNOMED CT for clinical concepts, RxNorm for medications, ICD-10-CM for diagnoses, DICOM for imaging. The subject is the RECORD, not AI: AI appears only as brief context (records are what any downstream tool consumes; representation quality bounds tool reliability). Every named fact, definition, standard, and example MUST come from the provided source excerpts; never invent an example, statistic, or citation. When citing a named source or standard, its URL from the excerpts appears on the slide.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Visual-first, punchy slides modeled on the client's own decks — NEVER walls of bullets. Most slides carry ONE idea in at most 30 words of body text: a big statement, a short quoted dialogue, a figure with a two-line explanation, or a compact table. Directly under each frame title, put a one-line italic message stating the slide's takeaway (like 'A number without its metadata is not information'). When a figure from the source excerpts fits the slide, the figure DOMINATES the slide (most of its width) with at most two short lines of text beside or below it. The lecture script carries the depth and nuance; the slides carry the punch. Open every session with a real hook from the sources; one discussion-cases slide per session; light humor welcome.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess record literacy: reading a value with its metadata, identifying what makes a record trustworthy or incomplete, matching record types to the standard that structures them. No exams, no coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: Explain what the medical record is (and is not) in plain language; name the major record types and the systems they live in; explain why a value without its metadata is not information, using real examples; describe how unstructured record text maps to structured concepts (entity recognition, negation, concept normalization); and match each record type to its standard (FHIR, OMOP, LOINC, SNOMED CT, RxNorm, ICD-10-CM, DICOM).
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline: Clinical Records — what the record is and how it is structured: Session 1 — the medical record itself, taught through the real documents: what legally and practically defines the medical record (the legal record, the designated record set, the EHR); the fundamentals of good record documentation; one patient, many systems (the information ecosystem: EHR, laboratory, pharmacy, imaging archive/PACS, monitoring, portal); why a recorded value needs its metadata to be information at all; how unstructured note text maps to structured clinical concepts; and a first tour of the standards that structure records (FHIR, OMOP, LOINC, RxNorm, DICOM) — with AI mentioned only as context, never as the subject; Session 2 — documentation and notes in depth; Session 3 — laboratory data and LOINC; Session 4 — imaging records, PACS, and DICOM; Session 5 — medications and RxNorm; Session 6 — exchange and research: FHIR and OMOP; with record quality, provenance, and interpretability applied throughout

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Record Reading (40%) — given a real record fragment (a value, a note excerpt, a header), identify what is missing to interpret it safely and what the metadata or standard adds. Mapping Exercise (35%) — match record types to the systems they live in and the standards that structure them; walk one unstructured-to-structured mapping. Discussion participation (25%) — engage the no-clean-answer record cases.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Short applied deliverables submitted via the learning platform.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Institution-approved learning platform; accessibility standards; no patient-identifiable information. Named tools, studies, and device cases are permitted when drawn from the provided public sources with attribution.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; no teaching assistant assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development delivered as ~1-hour daily sessions; this demo module spans 5-6 such sessions built around real cases, vignettes, and discussion.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for health-data literacy and responsible use of clinical information systems.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: All named examples, statistics, and cases must be traceable to the provided public sources (attribution on slide); no fabricated content; no patient-identifiable information; clinical-ethics norms respected.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Module must include learning outcomes, session structure, the assessment approach, and a sources page listing every cited source with its URL.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: Revision after client review: the previous module taught AI-safety cases when the client wanted the RECORD TYPES as the subject. This module is about clinical records; examples must be record examples (values, notes, headers, mappings), not AI examples. Grounding sources were provided by the client for exactly this topic.

session_structure: Each chapter of this course IS one one-hour session; the deck must be a lean, self-contained hour built AROUND worked record examples, with at most a third of the slides conceptual. Open with the session's real record moment, close with a knowledge check (answers on the following slide), 24-30 slides.
engagement_style: Teach the RECORD as the subject with ONE THING PER SLIDE — every slide holds exactly one definition-in-use, one worked record example, one table, or one question, sized to fill the page; never combine two ideas: (1) THE FIRST CONTENT SLIDE after the title must BE a real record moment from the excerpts (a real definitional line, a documentation rule, or a concrete record artifact) --- never an abstract framework. (2) WORKED RECORD EXAMPLES are the backbone --- include 4-5, each on its OWN slide, in the pattern: show a small real record fragment or value, ask what is missing to interpret it, then walk what the metadata or standard adds. Example shapes from the sources: a lab value and the metadata that makes it interpretable; a note sentence mapped to structured concepts with negation handled; an imaging file's header fields and what they carry; a medication entry normalized across vocabularies. (3) Include one 'One patient, many systems' TABLE slide: rows = record types (notes, labs, imaging, medications), columns = where it lives and which standard structures it (rendered with the LaTeX colorbox command as short chips: light-green for the standard, light-blue for the system). (4) Include 1-2 RECORD-READING SCENARIOS on their own slides: short realistic moments (a clinician reads a copied-forward note; a value arrives without units) with blocks 'The record shows' and 'The reader must ask', ending in a one-line takeaway. (5) Include one PROVENANCE QUESTIONS slide: the short questions a careful reader asks of any recorded value (where it originated, why it was collected, when it was recorded, whether it was transformed, whether it reflects the patient's current state) — drawn from the excerpts' guidance on documentation and provenance, phrased as questions. (6) One DISCUSSION CASES slide: 3-4 numbered one-line judgment scenarios about records with no clean answer. (7) CLOSE with a KNOWLEDGE CHECK of exactly 3 short questions --- questions ONLY; answers belong on the FOLLOWING slide. (8) At most 4 purely conceptual slides in the whole deck; AI may be mentioned on at most 2 slides as context (records feed downstream tools; representation quality bounds reliability) and never as a slide's subject. (9) LENGTH: 24-30 slides total, hard cap 40; exactly ONE Learning Objectives slide and ONE Key Takeaways slide; no two slides may restate the same point. (10) TONE: slide titles are active and curiosity-driven ('A number is not information'), never bureaucratic; the deck must FEEL like being taught to read records, not briefed about them. (11) REGISTER: the audience is practicing clinicians and healthcare staff --- never the words 'students' or 'textbook'. (12) VISUALS: use ONLY real figures present in the retrieved excerpts, each on its own slide (0.75+ textwidth, at most two short lines of text). (13) When a slide cites a named standard, article, or organization, put its SOURCE URL from the excerpts at the bottom. (14) NEVER invent a named example, number, quote, or citation --- if it is not in the excerpts, teach it generically or leave it out.
